questions.question: What does a materialized view store?
options: The SQL text of the query, recomputed in full on every request that reads it
The precomputed results of a supported query, refreshed as base data changes
A copy of the base table's rows, kept byte-identical and refreshed on a schedule
An in-memory cache of the query's result, discarded when the reservation restarts

questions.question: What is BigQuery smart tuning?
options: Automatic assignment of extra slots to any query that reads a materialized view
Background reordering of a base table's rows so the view's filters prune blocks
Automatic creation of a materialized view for any query the optimizer sees repeated
Optimizer rewriting of a base-table query to use a compatible materialized view

questions.question: Why align a materialized view partition with its base table?
options: Only the affected partitions need refreshing rather than the whole cached result
Alignment is what allows the optimizer to consider the view for smart tuning at all
Alignment removes the staleness window, so the view always reflects the newest rows
Alignment lets the view be stored in BI Engine memory instead of on Colossus

questions.question: What does BI Engine primarily provide?
options: A separate slot pool that runs dashboard queries ahead of the ETL reservation
A columnar rewrite of base tables on disk so every scan reads fewer stored bytes
In-memory caching and vectorized execution for the query stages a reservation supports
A managed cache of query results keyed by SQL text, reused for identical queries

questions.question: How should an engineer verify that smart tuning used a materialized view?
options: Compare the query's runtime against the same query run before the view existed
Confirm that the view's columns are a superset of the ones the query selects
Read the job's query plan and the materialized-view statistics it reports
Check that the query's result row count matches the view's stored row count

questions.question: Why can a query remain slow even with BI Engine enabled?
options: Only supported stages are accelerated, and the reservation can be under pressure
BI Engine only accelerates queries that already read a materialized view
BI Engine caches results but re-validates every cached row against the base table
BI Engine acceleration only applies after a query has run at least a hundred times

questions.question: What should query troubleshooting examine first?
options: The total wall-clock time of the job, which identifies which stage was the bottleneck
The job details and execution graph, with stage timing, bytes, and slot time
The table's schema and column types, which determine how the planner orders stages
The reservation's baseline setting, which fixes how many slots each stage receives

questions.question: Does LIMIT alone guarantee fewer bytes scanned?
options: No, because the scan that feeds the limit still reads every byte of required input
Yes, the engine stops reading storage as soon as the row count is satisfied
Yes, but only when the limit is smaller than one partition's worth of rows
No, but only for clustered tables, where block pruning happens after the limit

questions.question: Which change most directly reduces scan bytes?
options: Raising the reservation's max so more slots read the same bytes in parallel
Adding a LIMIT clause so the engine stops after enough rows have been produced
Ordering the results by the partition column so the planner can skip later blocks
Selecting only needed columns and filtering on a pruneable partition column

questions.question: What does a hot join key usually cause?
options: A broadcast join, since the planner copies the hot key's rows to every worker
Skew in the shuffle, with one straggler worker holding most of that key's rows
A full table scan, since the planner abandons partition pruning once a key dominates
An automatic re-cluster of the table, which pauses the query until sorting finishes

questions.question: A query spends most wall time waiting before execution while slots are saturated. What is the likely issue?
options: Shuffle skew, since one straggler partition holds the job open after its stage begins
Missing partition pruning, since the planner reads metadata for every partition first
Capacity contention, with the job queued behind other work on the same reservation
A cold BI Engine cache, which must be repopulated before any stage is scheduled

questions.question: Why can breaking one huge SQL statement into staged results help?
options: It removes the shuffle tier entirely, since each stage writes its output to storage
It guarantees lower total cost, because intermediate tables are never scanned twice
It removes the need for a dry run, since each staged table reports its own size
It lowers plan complexity, allows reuse, and localizes which stage went wrong

questions.question: What is BigQuery ML's main value?
options: Creating, evaluating, and using supported models in SQL, right where the data lives
Removing the need for train and test splits, since SQL evaluates the whole table
Exporting warehouse tables into Vertex AI so custom training frameworks can run
Serving models at single-digit millisecond latency for online prediction traffic

questions.question: Which task still requires careful design with BigQuery ML?
options: Writing the gradient-descent loop, since SQL cannot express iterative training
Sizing the slot reservation, since a CREATE MODEL statement cannot use autoscaling
Temporal splitting and point-in-time features that avoid leaking the future
Hand-encoding categorical columns, since BigQuery ML rejects any non-numeric input

questions.question: When is BigQuery ML a strong baseline choice?
options: When the model needs custom layers and a hand-written training loop running on GPUs
When the data is already SQL-accessible and a supported family fits the problem
When labels are unavailable and the goal is to discover them during training
When predictions must be served to a mobile app within a few milliseconds

questions.question: What should a reproducible BigQuery ML run record?
options: The dataset snapshot, training query, options, preprocessing, and eval split
The model name, its creation timestamp, and the final aggregate accuracy figure
The slot reservation used, the job ID, and the total bytes the training job read
The region, the connection ID, and the IAM roles granted on prediction outputs

questions.question: Why can random row splits produce misleading evaluation?
options: Random assignment leaves the classes unbalanced, so accuracy is no longer defined
Random splits force a full table scan, so the metrics get computed twice over
Random sampling drops rows with null features, shrinking the evaluation set
Future rows and rows from the same entity can land on both sides of the split

questions.question: What is the best response to one strong aggregate evaluation metric?
options: Retrain on the combined train and test rows so the deployed model sees everything
Break the metric down by relevant slice and check for leakage before trusting it
Raise the decision threshold until the minority class reaches the same score
Publish the model and monitor only the aggregate metric on live traffic

questions.question: What does ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING return for compatible input?
options: An embedding array for each input row, together with status fields that must be checked
A single embedding for the whole query result, computed after rows are aggregated
A distance score between each row's text and the model's nearest training example
A vector index over the source column, built in place and refreshed as rows change

questions.question: What does VECTOR_SEARCH do?
options: Rewrites a text predicate into a keyword search over the base table's search index
Builds the ANN structure that later queries use to avoid scanning every vector
Returns the nearest embeddings in a base table to a query vector, with distances
Normalizes a table's embedding column so that all compared vectors share one metric

questions.question: Why must row-level remote inference status be checked?
options: The status field carries the distance metric that a later vector search applies
A job can finish successfully while individual rows failed on quota or input
Rows that lack a status field are silently dropped from the destination table
The status field records which model revision produced each embedding row

questions.question: What changes when VECTOR_SEARCH uses a vector index?
options: Search becomes approximate, trading some recall for a much lower scan cost per query
Search becomes exact, since the index stores every pairwise distance in advance
Search results are restricted to rows whose metadata filter is evaluated first
Search switches to the query result cache, so repeated queries return instantly

questions.question: How should approximate vector-index quality be measured?
options: Count the rows the index covers and confirm the number matches the base table
Compare the index's top-k against brute-force results on sampled queries
Measure the latency drop against the same query run before the index existed
Check that the distance values returned fall inside the metric's expected range

questions.question: Why must model revision and output dimensionality be part of embedding lineage?
options: They set the partition column the embedding table uses for its daily refresh
They determine which BI Engine reservation the vector search draws memory from
Vectors from a different model or dimension no longer share a comparable space
They control how many candidates the approximate search returns per query row

questions.topic: Preparing Unstructured Data for Embeddings and RAG
questions.question: What does a BigQuery object table primarily represent?
options: A managed copy of each object's bytes, loaded into BigQuery's columnar storage
An external table whose rows are the parsed text extracted from each document
A staging table that Dataflow writes chunk records into before embeddings run
A read-only metadata index over Cloud Storage objects, with no parsed text

questions.topic: Preparing Unstructured Data for Embeddings and RAG
questions.question: What must parsing preserve for grounded citations?
options: The source version plus the page, block, or character span each chunk came from
The original file's storage class and the timestamp of its last lifecycle move
The token count of every chunk so the prompt builder can enforce its budget
The embedding model's revision, so the citation names which model retrieved it

questions.topic: Preparing Unstructured Data for Embeddings and RAG
questions.question: Which identity should an embedding row carry?
options: The request timestamp and the job ID of the query that generated the embedding
A stable chunk ID, its source-version ID, and the model version that made it
The dataset and table names, which together identify where the vector is stored
The distance metric the vector index uses, so later searches stay consistent

questions.topic: Preparing Unstructured Data for Embeddings and RAG
questions.question: Why deduplicate overlapping retrieved chunks before prompt construction?
options: Duplicate chunks break the citation format, since two spans cannot share a source
Overlapping chunks are always the result of a chunker bug that must be fixed first
Repeated text burns through the token budget and overweights a single piece of evidence
Duplicates inflate the vector index, so the approximate search loses recall on them

questions.topic: Preparing Unstructured Data for Embeddings and RAG
questions.question: Which layered evaluation best diagnoses a weak RAG answer?
options: Score the final answer against a human rating and tune the prompt until it rises
Score retrieval recall alone, since generation quality follows from good candidates
Score the embedding model on a public benchmark and swap it if it ranks poorly
Score parsing, chunking, embedding, retrieval, citation, and grounding separately

questions.topic: Preparing Unstructured Data for Embeddings and RAG
questions.question: When might external processing remain appropriate despite warehouse-native features?
options: When the corpus is small enough that a vector index would not be populated at all
When governance requires the data and its lineage to stay inside one product
When the source documents already live in Cloud Storage rather than in tables
When parsing is complex, serving must be fast, or ANN behavior must be tuned
